explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD tells Moses, Israel's leader, that Aaron, Israel's high priest, must not enter freely, “…or else he will die…” (Leviticus 16:2). That is plain and serious. Notice the word “freely,” too. The rest of the chapter spells out exactly how Aaron does go in.

Close, but that's not what the verse says. Nobody gets walked to the door here. The LORD says, “…or else he will die…” (Leviticus 16:2). Getting sent away would be the easy version, friend, and the text doesn't offer it.

Robes do show up in this chapter, but never as the penalty. The penalty in verse 2 is that Aaron “…will die…” Holy linen garments come in a couple of verses later, as part of how Aaron enters (Leviticus 16:4). Losing your outfit is a rough day, but this warning is far heavier than that.

Not quite, baker. Verse 4 calls these holy garments and says, “…he must bathe himself with water before he wears them.” So the bath comes first, and the linen comes second. Same as washing your hands before you touch the dough, only this time the LORD is giving the instructions.

That's right. Leviticus 16:4 says, “…he must bathe himself with water before he wears them.” The garments are holy, so Aaron washes first. Order matters in this chapter, friend, and this is the very first step you can see him taking.

Yes, baker. The text says Aaron is to present the bull “…and make atonement for himself and his household” (Leviticus 16:6). So the first sin offering covers Aaron and his own house. The people's sin offering comes later, with a goat (Leviticus 16:15).

Elders never come up in this passage, friend. Verse 6 says the bull is for Aaron, “…for himself and his household.” The people as a whole are covered later by the goat for the sin offering (Leviticus 16:15). Nobody gets added to the list that the text doesn't add.

Moses is the one hearing the LORD's instructions, but he isn't the one named for this bull. The verse says Aaron makes atonement “…for himself and his household” (Leviticus 16:6). It's Aaron's bull and Aaron's household. Moses gets to stand there and take notes.

explanations.answer: It is sent into the wilderness
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The scapegoat is presented alive before the LORD “…to make atonement by sending it into the wilderness as the scapegoat” (Leviticus 16:10). One goat is sacrificed and the other is sent away alive. Two goats, two different jobs.

explanations.answer: It is sacrificed on the altar
explanations.explanation: That's the other goat's job, friend. The goat chosen by lot for the LORD is the one sacrificed as a sin offering (Leviticus 16:9). The scapegoat is presented alive instead. Easy to mix up two goats on one chapter.

explanations.answer: It is kept at the Tent of Meeting
explanations.explanation: The text sends this goat the other direction. It's presented alive, and then it goes “…into the wilderness as the scapegoat” (Leviticus 16:10). Nobody gets a goat stall at the Tent of Meeting in this passage. This goat is headed out of town.

You got it, baker. Verse 13 says the cloud of incense “…will cover the mercy seat above the Testimony…” This is the same mercy seat from verse 2, where the LORD says He appears in the cloud. Aaron brings the incense to the place the LORD named.

The altar does show up in this chapter, but not here. Aaron takes burning coals from the altar (Leviticus 16:12), then goes inside the veil. The cloud of incense covers “…the mercy seat above the Testimony…” (Leviticus 16:13). The coals come from one place and the cloud lands in another.

No lampstand in this passage, friend. Verse 13 says the incense cloud covers “…the mercy seat above the Testimony…” Aaron puts the incense on the fire before the LORD, and the cloud settles over the mercy seat. The lampstand is not in this scene.

That's right, baker. Leviticus 16:13 says the cloud of incense will cover the mercy seat, “…so that he will not die.” That ties right back to the warning in verse 2. Aaron brings the incense in with him, and the cloud is there for his sake.

The verse says the opposite, friend. After Aaron puts the incense on the fire, the cloud covers the mercy seat “…so that he will not die” (Leviticus 16:13). The incense is part of how he goes in alive. The text says it plainly, so we can too.

explanations.answer: He sprinkles it like the bull's blood
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. The text says Aaron “…must do as he did with the bull's blood: He is to sprinkle it against the mercy seat and in front of it” (Leviticus 16:15). Same move, different animal. The bull was for his own sin offering and this goat is for the people's.

explanations.answer: He pours it out beside the ark
explanations.explanation: No pouring in this verse, friend. Aaron does with the goat's blood what he did with the bull's: “…He is to sprinkle it against the mercy seat and in front of it” (Leviticus 16:15). The sprinkling is the repeat. The ark isn't where the blood ends up in this verse.

explanations.answer: He mixes it into the incense
explanations.explanation: The incense has its own job, baker. It goes on the fire so the cloud covers the mercy seat (Leviticus 16:13). The goat's blood is sprinkled “…against the mercy seat and in front of it” (Leviticus 16:15). Incense in one hand and blood in the other, and the two never get stirred together.

You got it, baker. The LORD says Aaron makes atonement for the Most Holy Place “…because of the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins” (Leviticus 16:16). The text names the Israelites and says all their sins. Even the holy place is part of this.

explanations.answer: The sins of the nations nearby
explanations.explanation: Not in this verse, friend. The reason given is “…the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins” (Leviticus 16:16). The text names the Israelites, and no nearby nations come up. Stick with who the verse names.

explanations.answer: The sins of the people of Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt never shows up in this chapter, baker. Verse 16 gives the reason as “…the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins.” That is the reason for the Most Holy Place. Egypt isn't on the guest list.

Not quite, baker. Leviticus 16:17 says, “No one may be in the Tent of Meeting from the time Aaron goes in to make atonement in the Most Holy Place until he leaves…” So nobody is in there with him. It's Aaron going in, and everyone else stays out.

That's right. Verse 17 says, “No one may be in the Tent of Meeting from the time Aaron goes in to make atonement in the Most Holy Place until he leaves…” That covers the whole time he is making atonement for himself, his household and the whole assembly of Israel. Aaron goes in, and the Tent of Meeting stays empty of everyone else.

explanations.answer: To cleanse it from Israel's uncleanness
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Aaron sprinkles the blood seven times “…to cleanse it and consecrate it from the uncleanness of the Israelites” (Leviticus 16:19). The altar gets cleansed and consecrated, the same as the Most Holy Place and the Tent of Meeting. The blood is the cleaning supply here, and I promise it's not a cookie sheet.

explanations.answer: To mark it for the next high priest
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that, friend. Verse 19 gives the reason: “…to cleanse it and consecrate it from the uncleanness of the Israelites.” The next high priest does come up later in the chapter (Leviticus 16:32), but not as the reason for the blood on the altar. The verse tells us what it's for, so we go with that.

explanations.answer: To warn the people to stay back
explanations.explanation: No warning is mentioned here, baker. The verse says Aaron sprinkles the blood “…to cleanse it and consecrate it from the uncleanness of the Israelites” (Leviticus 16:19). It's about the altar being cleansed. The people being kept back isn't the reason the text gives.

explanations.answer: He confesses all Israel's sins over it
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Aaron lays both hands on the live goat's head and confesses over it “…all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins” (Leviticus 16:21). Then he puts them on the goat's head and sends it away. That's a lot to say out loud in one sitting.

explanations.answer: He ties a scarlet cord on its horns
explanations.explanation: No cord in this passage, friend. After laying both hands on the goat's head, Aaron is to “…confess over it all the iniquities and rebellious acts of the Israelites in regard to all their sins” (Leviticus 16:21). It's hands and words. Nothing gets tied on.

explanations.answer: He anoints its head with oil
explanations.explanation: Oil isn't in the verse, baker. What Aaron does is lay both hands on the goat's head and confess over it all the iniquities of the Israelites (Leviticus 16:21). Then he puts them on the goat's head. It's a confession, and no anointing.

explanations.answer: His burnt offering and the people's
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Once he's in his own clothes, Aaron goes out and sacrifices “…his burnt offering and the people's burnt offering to make atonement for himself and for the people” (Leviticus 16:24). The people have their burnt offering too. Both are done in his regular clothes, after the bath.

explanations.answer: A second bull for the people
explanations.explanation: No second bull here, friend. The bull was for Aaron's own sin offering (Leviticus 16:11), and the people's sin offering was a goat (Leviticus 16:15). In verse 24, the offerings are “…his burnt offering and the people's burnt offering.” Count carefully, because this chapter has a lot of animals.

explanations.answer: A lamb for the other priests
explanations.explanation: No lamb shows up in this passage, baker. Verse 24 says Aaron sacrifices “…his burnt offering and the people's burnt offering to make atonement for himself and for the people.” A lamb for other priests isn't named. Stay with what the verse lists.

That's right, baker. The man who released the goat “…must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water; afterward he may reenter the camp” (Leviticus 16:26). Clothes first, then the bath, then he's back in. Walking a goat into a solitary place is a job that ends with laundry.

No waiting period in this verse, friend. The text says he “…must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water; afterward he may reenter the camp” (Leviticus 16:26). So it's a wash, then right back in. Seven days is a number from somewhere else in the chapter, not this verse.

explanations.answer: Bring an offering of his own
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't ask him for an offering, baker. It says he “…must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water; afterward he may reenter the camp” (Leviticus 16:26). What he does is wash, and then he comes back in. No extra animals needed.
You got it, baker. The bull and the goat are taken outside the camp, “…and their hides, flesh, and dung must be burned up” (Leviticus 16:27). Nothing is left behind. It all goes up.

Not quite, friend. Verse 27 says the bull and the goat are taken outside the camp, “…and their hides, flesh, and dung must be burned up.” Fire is the word, and no digging is mentioned. No shovels are needed for this one.

explanations.answer: Everything left goes to the priests
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't hand any of it to the priests, baker. It says the bull and the goat are taken outside the camp, “…and their hides, flesh, and dung must be burned up” (Leviticus 16:27). Burned up means burned up. Nobody is carrying leftovers home.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “…you shall humble yourselves and not do any work…” (Leviticus 16:29). Verse 31 repeats it: “…that you may humble yourselves…” The day is set apart, and humbling comes with it.

Treat yourself sounds nice, friend, but that's not the word. The verse says, “…you shall humble yourselves and not do any work…” (Leviticus 16:29). The people are to humble themselves on that day. No gift baskets.
Nobody is padding their bank account on this day, baker. Verse 29 says, “…you shall humble yourselves and not do any work…” With no work, there would be no paycheck anyway. The word is humble.

Not quite, baker. Verse 29 says the day is for you, “…whether the native or the foreigner who resides among you.” So the foreigner living among them is included. It isn't only for the native Israelites.

That's right. Leviticus 16:29 says that on the tenth day of the seventh month, no work gets done, “…whether the native or the foreigner who resides among you.” The foreigner living among them is included in the rule. Everybody takes the day.

explanations.answer: Atonement will be made to cleanse them
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD says, “…on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, and you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD” (Leviticus 16:30). That is the reason given. The whole day is about atonement and being made clean.

explanations.answer: It marks the day they left Egypt
explanations.explanation: Not in this passage, friend. The reason the LORD gives is that “…atonement will be made for you to cleanse you…” (Leviticus 16:30). Leaving Egypt isn't mentioned in this chapter. Stick with the reason in the verse.

explanations.answer: It marks the end of the harvest
explanations.explanation: Harvest never comes up here, baker. Verse 30 gives the reason: “…on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you, and you will be clean from all your sins before the LORD.” That's what makes the day big. The text doesn't connect it to a harvest.

explanations.answer: The priest ordained to succeed his father
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Verse 32 says, “The priest who is anointed and ordained to succeed his father as high priest shall make atonement.” So this isn't a one time job for Aaron. It gets passed on, and the next high priest puts on the sacred linen garments too.

explanations.answer: Whoever the elders of Israel choose
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't hand that choice to the elders, friend. It says, “The priest who is anointed and ordained to succeed his father as high priest shall make atonement” (Leviticus 16:32). The one who does it is the successor. Nobody is taking a vote in this passage.

explanations.answer: The oldest man from each tribe
explanations.explanation: No tribe lineup in this passage, baker. Verse 32 says the one who makes atonement is “The priest who is anointed and ordained to succeed his father as high priest…” It's a priest, in the high priest's line. Age isn't how the text says it is decided.

You got it, baker. The LORD says it is “…to make atonement once a year for the Israelites because of all their sins” (Leviticus 16:34). One day a year, and it's a permanent statute. That's why the tenth day of the seventh month matters so much.
Not twice, friend. Verse 34 says, “…to make atonement once a year for the Israelites because of all their sins.” One day, once a year. Twice would be a different chapter.

I see where that comes from, baker. Seven times does show up in this chapter, but it's the sprinkling of the blood (Leviticus 16:14, 19). For the statute itself, the LORD says, “…to make atonement once a year for the Israelites because of all their sins” (Leviticus 16:34). Seven sprinkles in a day, and one day a year.
